0: Author: Wu Chenfei, Qwen-image lead, ModelScope contributor
1: When preparing a chemistry lesson, to explain an experiment clearly, besides text descriptions, you can also add an image. For example, when teaching the experiment of putting an iron nail into a copper sulfate solution, you need to show the changes before and after the experiment, putting the reaction equation, experimental phenomena, and key knowledge points together so students can compare them side by side.
2: Can we ask an image generation model to help with this kind of work? We can organize the verified knowledge content, along with the visuals, text, and layout we want to present, into a detailed prompt, let the model try to generate the entire poster, and then check and adjust based on the results.
3: This chapter starts from this need and uses Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo to generate a chemistry knowledge poster.
5: Since its release, Qwen-Image-2.1 has received a lot of attention from the community. Qwen-Image-2.1 unifies text-to-image and image editing in a single model. The visual generation part of the model has only 7B parameters and uses a 32-layer Single-Stream DiT. It scored 60.28 on the official public Qwen-Image-Bench evaluation and natively supports transparent image generation and editing with up to 10 reference images. Community feedback has been positive, so we use this model as an example to run through deployment and a practical scenario.

15: PROMPT is the input prompt of the model, specifically the positive prompt here. Regarding prompts, we have three concepts: positive prompt, negative prompt, and user prompt. Let us explain them separately:
16: positive prompt: that is, "what you want", which is the PROMPT variable in this code. Here we describe what the target image should contain, its style, composition, and details. Generally speaking, the richer the positive prompt is written, the more controllable the generation effect becomes. Therefore, the positive prompt in our example is very detailed. The positive prompt is directly encoded by the text encoder, and then through the denoise process, Gaussian noise is "pulled" toward a distribution that matches the description.
17: negative prompt: that is, "what you don't want". The negative prompt is likewise directly encoded by the text encoder, and its effect is equivalent to making the model move away from the features described by the negative prompt. It should be specially noted here that there is no negative prompt in this script code. This is not an omission, but because Qwen-Image-2.1 (and of course Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo) has distilled away CFG to improve model inference efficiency, so there is no need to input a negative prompt.
18: user prompt: that is, "the sentence the user will actually type". In real scenarios, users will not write a thousand-word poster description; they will only say: "Help me draw a chemistry notes poster explaining iron displacing copper." The characteristics of a user prompt are: short, colloquial, multilingual, and low in information density. In contrast, the characteristics of the corresponding positive prompt are: long, structured, Chinese and English, and high in information density. Because models are generally trained on positive prompts (for better image-text alignment) rather than user prompts, user prompts are not suitable for direct use. Usually, a language model is used to perform rewriting, turning the user prompt with the user's plain intent into a complete user prompt with style, composition, and details. In addition, for professional AIGC designers, they can directly manually write their user prompt intent into a high-quality positive prompt, which is often better than automatic rewriting by a language model. It is worth mentioning that, to show the most streamlined code, we do not start image generation from the user prompt, but skip rewriting and start directly from the positive prompt.

46: This is a very common error. The free GPU provided by modelscope only has 24GiB of VRAM. Generally, following the image.py approach requires 57GiB. But don't worry, we can save VRAM by "shuffling" things around. We modified image.py and created a new file image_24G.py:
47: Let's explain a few modification points in this code:
48: [1] Load the pipeline, including Text Encoder, DiT, and VAE, onto the CPU.
50: When enable_tiling is turned on, the VAE decoder performs inference in tiles of 256*256 pixels each, with a stride of 192, adjacent tiles overlapping by 64 pixels, plus linear blending at the seams. Since the decoder only processes one tile at a time, the activation peak during decoding drops significantly. Of course, this is not lossless—if VRAM is sufficient, turning off tiling yields the best results.
51: [3] Put the Text Encoder on the GPU first to compute the text representation
52: [4] Move the Text Encoder back to the CPU and return the GPU cache to the driver.
53: [5] Put DiT and VAE on the GPU to compute the generated image
54: Actually, diffusers has a built-in function for this kind of shuffling between CPU and GPU, called enable_model_cpu_offload(). Readers can try it themselves.
55: Finally, we can also put the code into Jupyter for more agile testing, avoiding reloading the model on every inference in image_24G.py.

104: 1. Preparation and testing of carbon dioxide: first explain clearly how the apparatus is connected
105: This example needs to place "producing gas" and "testing gas" on the same information path: the reaction occurs in the conical flask on the left, the gas passes through the delivery tube, and produces a visible change in the limewater on the right.
106: Before drawing, you can first fix two equations:
107: Calcium carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce carbon dioxide; when carbon dioxide is passed into clear limewater, calcium carbonate precipitate can form, making the liquid turbid. Royal Society of Chemistry teaching resources, Indiana University chemistry demonstrations
108: This image only shows the stage where a small amount of carbon dioxide is passed in and the limewater turns cloudy. The prompt should also explain two details that are easy to draw incorrectly: the outlet of the gas delivery tube in the generation apparatus is above the liquid surface, and the end of the tube in the testing apparatus extends below the surface of the limewater; the receiving test tube remains open.
109: Prompt that can be copied directly:
111: Visual check: In this result, the preparation and testing equations are legible; the end of the gas delivery tube in the generation apparatus is above the liquid surface, the testing end extends below the liquid surface, and the receiving test tube remains open. The generated image omits the support stand; it can be used as a schematic of the apparatus relationships, and the method of fixing the equipment should be explained additionally during teaching.
112: 2. Acid-base neutralization and phenolphthalein color change: draw the change, and also preserve the boundary of judgment
113: Color changes are suitable for expression through before-and-after comparison. We have the left beaker show dilute sodium hydroxide solution with phenolphthalein added, and the right side show the state after dilute hydrochloric acid is added dropwise, with the pink color gradually fading. The reaction to be presented in the poster is:
114: When hydrochloric acid is added dropwise to sodium hydroxide solution containing phenolphthalein, disappearance of the pink color can be observed. Oxford University Chemistry Demonstration
115: A statement must be specially retained here: the fading of phenolphthalein cannot by itself prove that the solution has been exactly completely neutralized, nor can pH=7 be judged merely from being colorless. Indicator color change reflects the indicator's own state as solution conditions change; in university teaching demonstrations, acid is also continuously added to switch the system between acidic and alkaline states. University of Colorado Teaching Demonstration Therefore, we write this statement directly into the poster, rather than letting the model add on its own the conclusion that "turning colorless means neutral."
117: Visual check: This result presents a comparison from pink solution to colorless solution, and the dilute hydrochloric acid in the dropper and the falling droplets remain colorless. The neutralization equation, ionic equation, and the statement that "pH=7 cannot be judged merely from being colorless" are legible.
118: 3. How the blue precipitate appears: draw the difference between "solution" and "solid"
119: The focus of this experiment is to let students distinguish a uniform transparent blue solution from an insoluble blue precipitate. Adding sodium hydroxide solution to copper sulfate solution forms a blue copper hydroxide precipitate. Rwanda Education Board Chemistry Experiment Manual
120: We divide the image into three states: "before reaction—adding reagent—after standing," and explicitly require drawing a blue flocculent solid. The final state in the image is set as having added enough NaOH to precipitate most of the copper ions; in actual experiments, the color of the upper liquid also depends on conditions such as the amount of reagent used. This example is not heated, and no bubbles or flames need to be drawn.
122: Visual check: This result presents separately the blue transparent solution, the formation of blue flocculent precipitate, and the state after standing when the precipitate has gathered; the NaOH dropper and falling droplets remain colorless, and the two equations are legible. The upper liquid after standing is drawn as nearly colorless, corresponding to the setting of "adding enough NaOH" in this example.

Fixing the random seed helps compare changes before and after revision, but it does not guarantee pixel-by-pixel consistency across devices or versions.

127: These examples also remind us: a prompt states the requirements, but you still need to check each item after generation. Before using it in class, you can check with three questions: are the equations and text correct, do the equipment and labels correspond, and does the image support the conclusions in the body text? When a single image cannot hold all the content, you can reduce the text, or split it into two images—an "experimental phenomena diagram" and a "principle explanation diagram"—and then compare them.
